title: the whole first instruction: in, out
hook: the whole first instruction: in, out

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, friendliness, from the word for a friend. Your line was may you be at ease. Did someone annoying get one quiet wish? Day two.

People imagine meditation is hard to start. You need a cushion, an app, incense, a retreat in the mountains, a mind that goes blank on command. Then you actually read how the Buddha is remembered teaching it, and the first instruction is almost funny in how small it is. Sit down. Breathe in, and know you're breathing in. Breathe out, and know you're breathing out. That's it. That's the doorway. And the one thing it needs, you've been doing all day without being asked, since the minute you were born. Today's word is the oldest meditation object there is.
screen: `NO CUSHION REQUIRED.` → `IN, AND KNOW IT.` → `OUT, AND KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: The breath. In the old Pali texts, the practice is called anapanasati: mindfulness of breathing in and breathing out. There's a whole discourse on it, and it begins with a scene. A monk goes to the forest, or the foot of a tree, or an empty room. He sits down, crosses his legs, keeps his body upright, and sets his attention right in front of him. Then, mindful, he breathes in. Mindful, he breathes out. Breathing a long breath, he knows it's long. Breathing a short breath, he knows it's short. Notice what's missing. Nobody tells him to breathe in a special way. No counting to four, no holding, no fixing. The breath is left exactly as it is. The job is only to know it. That's a quiet revolution, because most of us spend the day not knowing we're breathing at all. Why the breath? Teachers give a few reasons. It's always with you, so you can practice on a bus. It's always now; you can't breathe yesterday's breath. And it sits right on the line between what you do and what just happens, so watching it teaches you something about both. The discourse goes on for sixteen steps, from the breath to the body, to feelings, to the mind, to the deepest things the Buddha taught. But every one of those steps is still riding on the same in and out. Across Buddhist countries and schools, Zen, Tibetan, Theravada, the breath shows up again and again as a place to begin. Not because it's special. Because it's already here.
screen: `ANAPANASATI — BREATHING IN, OUT.` · `A TREE, A SEAT, AN UPRIGHT BODY.` · `LONG, KNOW IT'S LONG.` · `ALWAYS WITH YOU, ALWAYS NOW.` · then, large: `YOU'RE ALREADY DOING IT.`

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. Don't change anything. Don't make it deep or slow or impressive. Just let the next breath come in, and know it's coming in. Feel where it's easiest to notice: the nose, the chest, the belly. Then let it go out, and know it's going out. One whole breath, known from start to finish. That's the entire first instruction, done.
The breath. The first meditation object, always with you, always now. Breathing in, knowing it. Second word.
Your line: you're already doing it. Three times today, at a red light, in a line, before you open a message, notice one breath all the way through. Day two.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists begin meditation by sitting upright and simply paying attention to the natural breath as it comes in and goes out, in monasteries, meditation halls and at home, often for a set time marked by a bell.

fork.setup: you sit down to meditate for the first time. your breath is short and a bit shaky. what does the old instruction say to do?

original.note: Pali: mindfulness (sati) of breathing in and out (ānāpāna).

trapdoor: what it means: letting the breath be as it is and simply knowing it, in and out.
what a scholar hears: ānāpānasati, the practice of the Anapanasati Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 118): sixteen steps that move from breath to body, feeling, mind and insight.

sources.ref: Maha Satipatthana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 22), the section on breathing

notes: The opening scene (forest, root of a tree, empty hut; sits cross-legged, body upright, mindfulness 'in front'; long and short breaths) is paraphrased from MN 118 and DN 22. Confirm.
The reasons for choosing the breath (always present, always now, between voluntary and involuntary) are a general teachers' summary, not a single text. Confirm acceptable.
Which of āna/apāna is in-breath and which is out-breath is debated by commentators; the script avoids splitting them. Confirm the Devanagari and pronunciation.
